title: What Do Foreign Trends Tell Us About Future U.S. Labor Force Dynamics? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed economists show that from 2014-2025 advanced-economy labor forces kept growing despite shrinking working-age populations thanks to rising female and older-worker participation, while immigration alone drove working-age population growth. With U.S. net immigration collapsing and participation gains finite (Korea previews the post-2028 exhaustion), U.S. labor supply may soon shrink and will hinge on immigration and participation policy.

insights.claim: U.S. working-age population growth has fallen to near zero after a sharp drop in net immigration, and with the native-born working-age population already declining, U.S. available labor supply could soon begin to shrink.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: A shrinking labor supply caps potential GDP growth and keeps labor markets tight, supporting wage pressure and a structurally higher neutral-rate debate.
insights.quote: Growth in the U.S. working-age population has fallen to near zero with the recent sharp drop in net immigration.

insights.claim: NY Fed economists argue the demographic headwinds that hit advanced economies with faster aging and lower immigration (e.g., Japan, Germany, Italy, Korea) are now coming into view for the U.S., making those economies a preview of the U.S. path.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Use Japan/Korea/Europe labor-market histories as analogs for how U.S. wages, participation and growth may evolve under low immigration.
insights.quote: the demographic headwinds long visible abroad may now be coming into clear view at home

insights.claim: From 2014 to 2025 the U.S. working-age (15-64) population grew 3.0%, prime-age (25-54) population 4.0%, and labor force 9.6% — solidly positive but not near the top of the advanced-economy distribution.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: The U.S. demographic advantage versus peers has been real but modest, and is eroding as immigration falls.
insights.locator: The first column shows wide variation

insights.claim: U.S. labor force participation gains since 2014 (+2.3 ppt for ages 15-64, +3.2 ppt for women, +0.5 ppt for ages 65-74) have lagged advanced-economy medians (+4, +5.2, +5.6 ppt) on all three dimensions.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Below-norm U.S. participation gains imply residual room to offset immigration losses — if policy or wages pull people in.
insights.quote: Note that participation gains in the U.S., while positive, have been below AE norms across all three dimensions of the participation data.
insights.locator: As shown in the first column, the trend

insights.claim: U.S. 2025 participation is 75% for ages 15-64 (versus an AE median of 78.6%), 70.3% for women 15-64 (median 75.4%), and a moderately high 26.7% for ages 65-74 (median 18.1%).
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: The U.S. gap is concentrated in prime working ages and women, not older workers — the margin where policy (childcare, etc.) could matter most.

insights.claim: Raising U.S. working-age participation to 85% — roughly the current AE frontier — would be mechanically equivalent to a roughly 13% increase in the engaged working-age population, though the authors stress the existence of this upside gives no reason to expect it will be tapped.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Treat participation upside as a theoretical buffer, not a forecast; labor-supply bulls relying on it face execution risk.
insights.quote: Of course, the fact that this upside exists provides no reason to believe that it will be tapped.

insights.claim: Across advanced economies from 2014 to 2025, labor forces grew even where working-age populations shrank: only Greece and Latvia saw small labor force declines in a 36-country sample, with a median AE labor force gain of 8.5% against a -1.4% working-age population change.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Shrinking populations have not yet translated into shrinking labor forces — the bite comes once participation tops out.
insights.quote: active populations have defied demographic gravity
insights.locator: The third column of the table

insights.claim: Japan's labor force grew 6% from 2014 to 2025 despite a roughly 7% drop in its working-age population, and Germany's grew almost 6% despite a 2% working-age decline and an over-8% drop in prime-age population.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Japan and Germany show participation can mask demographic decline for a decade — but those buffers are now largely used up.

insights.claim: Rising participation among women and the 'young old' (ages 65-74) drove AE labor-force resilience: Japan's female participation rose 11.2 ppt and its 65-74 participation 12.6 ppt since 2014, with Korea (+10.5 ppt) and the Netherlands (+9.8 ppt) close behind on older workers.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Female and older-worker participation is the key lever that kept aging economies' labor supply growing; watch for its exhaustion.

insights.claim: Japan (82.3%), the Netherlands (85.7%), Switzerland (84.1%) and Sweden (84%) lead AE working-age participation in 2025, while Italy is lowest at 66.7% — raising Italy to 85% would be like a 26% increase in its working-age population.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Italy holds the largest mechanical labor-supply upside among large AEs, a potential growth tailwind if reforms lift participation.
insights.locator: As shown in the first column, the median AE

insights.claim: Participation among 65-74 year-olds is strikingly heterogeneous: Korea (50.3%) and Japan (46.1%) are very high, while France (7.6%), Belgium (8%) and Spain (8.2%) are very low; because the 'young old' group is growing in relative size, gains there can have an outsized impact on aggregate labor force growth.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: European pension/retirement reforms that lift older-worker participation could be a meaningful labor-supply lever as this cohort swells.
insights.quote: increases in “young old” participation can have an outsized impact on aggregate labor force growth, given the growing relative size of this age group
insights.locator: The potential increase in the engaged

insights.claim: Participation gains are finite and cannot keep offsetting shrinking working-age populations indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Models extrapolating recent labor-force resilience in aging economies risk overstating future growth.
insights.quote: But participation rates can’t keep rising forever: Demography is eventually destiny.

insights.claim: Korea already sits at the AE frontier for 'young old' participation alongside Japan, leaving little remaining upside; with participation projected by the Bank of Korea to peak around 2028 and then decline, its participation buffer is likely to flip from an offset to a drag on labor force growth.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Expect Korean labor force growth to slow sharply after ~2028 — a headwind for Korean potential growth and a template for other low-immigration aging economies.
insights.quote: the participation buffer is likely to shift from an offset to a drag
insights.locator: Korea already sits at the AE frontier

insights.claim: Because Korea's net immigration remains limited and is not expected to rise materially, Korea offers a preview of how quickly labor force growth can slow once participation gains are exhausted.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Watch Korea as the leading indicator for what happens to labor supply when both the participation and immigration margins are closed.
insights.quote: Korea offers a preview of how quickly labor force growth can slow once participation gains are exhausted
insights.locator: Korea already sits at the AE frontier

insights.claim: Immigration, not fertility, explains why several advanced economies saw strong working-age population growth from 2014 to 2025; every AE except Israel had fertility below replacement by the early-to-mid 1970s.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: Working-age population growth in AEs is essentially an immigration-policy variable — track migration policy to forecast labor supply.
insights.quote: Immigration, not fecundity, is the explanation.

insights.claim: Every advanced economy whose working-age population rose from 2014 to 2025 recorded substantial net immigration equal to at least several percentage points of the initial working-age stock; Australia (+10.5%), Sweden (+8.3%) and Canada (+7.0%) posted the largest working-age gains.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: High-immigration economies like Australia and Canada have had the strongest labor force growth (24.0% and 18.3%), a tailwind to their potential output.
insights.locator: We don’t have good data on current migrant stocks

insights.claim: Relative to its size, the U.S. has not been a standout immigration destination: immigration did more to boost working-age populations in the UK, Sweden and Switzerland, among others.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: The U.S. has less of an immigration-driven buffer than commonly assumed, so cuts in net immigration bite quickly.
insights.quote: Notably, relative to its size, the U.S. does not particularly stand out as a destination.
insights.locator: We don’t have good data on current migrant stocks

insights.claim: China's labor force fell 3.9% from 2014 to 2025 as its working-age population declined 4.5% and prime-age population an estimated 9.7%, with working-age participation also down 2.2 ppt — unlike AEs, participation did not offset demographics.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: China is already in absolute labor-force decline, a structural drag on its potential growth.
insights.locator: Level-Setting AE Population and Labor Force Growth

insights.claim: Future U.S. labor supply will depend increasingly on policy choices around immigration and participation, since immigration has been the key driver of AE working-age growth and participation offsets are temporary.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey B. Dawson
insights.so_what: U.S. immigration policy is now a first-order macro variable for labor supply, potential growth, wages and inflation.
insights.quote: future labor supply will depend increasingly on policy choices around immigration and participation
